title: ARE WE UNDER GRACE OR STILL UNDER GOD'S LAW?
paragraphs: ARE WE UNDER GRACE OR STILL UNDER GOD'S LAW?
The question that has divided churches, confused believers, fueled arguments, and left millions wondering whether they are truly free... or secretly failing God every day.
There are few questions that expose the heart faster than this one.
Or are we still under God's Law?
The answer may be one of the most misunderstood truths in modern Christianity.
Many believers live trapped between two fears.
"If I focus too much on grace, I'll become careless with sin."
"If I don't keep enough rules, God won't accept me."
Trying to silence a question that never seems to leave:
That question is exactly why we must go back to Scripture.
Because the answer is far more beautiful than most people realize.
The ground trembles beneath your feet.
This is where God gives His Law.
The Hebrew word for law is תּוֹרָה (Torah).
Many people think Torah simply means "rules."
Its deeper meaning is instruction, teaching, guidance.
It revealed what righteousness looked like.
But it also revealed something else.
The Law was never merely a list of commands.
A divine mirror showing humanity exactly how far we had fallen.
Like an X-ray exposing a broken bone, the Law could reveal the problem but could never heal it.
This is why generation after generation offered sacrifices.
Blood flowed endlessly because sin remained.
When Jesus arrived, He spoke words that still create confusion today:
"Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them." (Matthew 5:17)
The Greek word used for fulfill is πληρόω (plēroō).
to complete, to bring to full measure, to accomplish perfectly.
Jesus did not destroy God's Law.
Every requirement found its perfection in Him.
The cross is where grace and justice kissed.
But because God punished sin in Christ.
The Greek word translated "end" is τέλος (telos).
But telos often means goal, culmination, fulfillment, intended destination.
Christ is what the Law was always leading toward.
Then comes one of the most quoted verses in the entire Bible:
"For sin shall not have dominion over you, because you are not under law but under grace." (Romans 6:14)
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (charis).
But this is where many stop reading.
"What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!" (Romans 6:15)
Grace is not permission to sin.
Grace is power to overcome sin.
The same grace that forgives also transforms.
The same grace that saves also sanctifies.
The same grace that rescues also changes.
This is where many Christians accidentally create a false choice.
They think there are only two options.
The other says God's love came first.
The prophet Jeremiah foretold a coming covenant centuries before Jesus arrived.
"I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts." (Jeremiah 31:33)
Before, commandments were written on stone.
Now they are written on hearts.
The believer does not obey to become accepted.
The believer obeys because they already are accepted in Christ.
This is why the New Testament repeatedly speaks of a new covenant.
The Greek phrase is καινὴ διαθήκη (kainē diathēkē).
A new covenant established through the blood of Jesus.
The old covenant depended upon human performance.
The new covenant depends upon Christ's finished work.
The other is sealed through the Spirit.
Some people hear this and ask:
"So does God's Law no longer matter?"
The Law still reveals God's character.
The Law still shows what pleases God.
But believers no longer seek justification through Law keeping.
That door has been permanently closed.
"By works of the law no human being will be justified." (Romans 3:20)
The Law can show us our need.
A lighthouse reveals where safety is.
But the lighthouse cannot pull you from the water.
Many people are trying to cling to the lighthouse.
God is pointing them to the Savior.
This is why some of the most exhausted Christians are those trying to earn what Jesus already purchased.
They know the language of grace.
Every weakness feels like God's disappointment.
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." (Romans 8:1)
The Hebrew concept of grace appears throughout the Old Testament in the word חֵן (chen).
Grace did not begin in the New Testament.
Grace was God's heartbeat from Genesis onward.
The cross simply revealed grace in its fullest expression.
Maybe that is why this conversation becomes so personal.
Because deep down, most people are not asking a theological question.
They are asking an emotional one.
"Can God really love someone like me?"
The Gospel answers with a bloodstained cross and an empty tomb.
So are Christians under grace or under God's Law?
We are not under the Law as a covenant of justification.
We are under Grace through Jesus Christ.
Yet grace does not produce rebellion.
Grace produces transformed hearts that love the God who saved them.
And when we belong to Christ, obedience becomes the fruit of salvation—not the price of salvation.
And for the believer, He still is.
The moment you stop trying to earn the cross is often the moment you finally understand it.
